prize_parts.citation: for the theory and first experimental realisation of circuit quantum electrodynamics, strong coupling of superconducting circuits to single microwave photons

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B040) first and circuit QED (B016) second, and having read the other seven ballots I now put circuit QED first. It is the only shortlisted candidate that every one of the eight members ranked, with first places from Johansson and Mehlig and top-three placements from Olsson, Lindroth and me, so the support does not rest on one subfield. The science is a clean, well-defined invention with a measurable signature: strong coupling of a superconducting qubit to a single microwave photon in 2004, dispersive readout, and the bus architecture on which superconducting processors are built. The attribution is as clear as any candidate offers: Blais for the theory proposal, and Wallraff and Schoelkopf for the 2004 strong-coupling experiments. Twenty years of independent replication leave no maturity doubt. Colleagues' arguments across the table agree on this point and I find them stronger than my own earlier ranking, which leaned on my instrumental affinity for IceCube.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is adjacency to the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which Danielsson, Kroll and Eriksson all flagged. A further circuit prize so soon may look like the same neighbourhood honoured twice, and the committee must be able to state clearly that light-matter coupling and readout architecture is a distinct discovery from macroscopic quantum coherence. There is also the credit boundary: Girvin and Huang were co-authors of the founding theory paper and the Yale experimental team was larger than two names, so any trio leaves someone out. Finally, a prize that rewards the platform for quantum computing risks being seen as rewarding technology rather than a discovery.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the natural successor to the 2025 circuit prize, with a clean Blais-Wallraff-Schoelkopf theory-plus-experiment trio, while acknowledging that he directs a related centre and may be biased.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the trio, but I would not treat succession to 2025 as a point in its favour. Following on from a recent award is a risk to manage, not a merit, and the citation has to rest on strong light-matter coupling and dispersive readout, not on the earlier tunnelling work. Because you work in this area, I would like the committee to hear a technical argument from you on what the architecture added beyond the macroscopic quantum phenomena already honoured, and on whether Girvin's role requires a different configuration. Your declared proximity is reason for the rest of us to test your enthusiasm, not to discount your expertise.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as the missing half of the 2013 award and ranks IceCube second, noting that source identification is still evolving and that circuit QED may overlap with 2025.
responses.response: On IceCube you are right that the diffuse flux is secure while source identification rests on a few objects, and that tempers my own first-place ranking. On the Higgs I respect the scientific weight but remain doubtful that three names can fairly represent ATLAS and CMS; we cannot set the collaboration question aside, and I ranked it seventh because of that. I therefore disagree that it should lead. On the overlap with 2025 I disagree with your lowest ranking for circuit QED: the 2025 work concerned macroscopic tunnelling, while this is a distinct architecture with its own experiment.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first, with a clean Katori and Ye pair, a two-decade record of confirmation and consequences for the redefinition of the second, and ranks circuit QED fourth because of its proximity to 2025.
responses.response: This is the strongest rival and I took it seriously: I placed clocks fifth, and the two-name attribution is cleaner than any other. My hesitation is novelty relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 trapped-ion prize, which you and Lindroth both noted. A prize whose citation will be read as a continuation of two earlier awards is more exposed than one opening a distinct architecture. I would, though, keep clocks as a close alternative, particularly if the redefinition of the second is adopted before the decision.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as an invention that changed a field, with a clear theory, realisation and application split among Rose, Haider and Urban, and ranks circuit QED second.
responses.response: I share your view that this is a decisive instrument invention with a clear trio, and as an instrument builder I do not dismiss instrumentation. Your own caveats weigh on me: the parallel STEM corrector line of Krivanek is outside the credited names, and you note the question of whether the committee sees this as physics. Since you ranked circuit QED second and I rank it first, I read our views as nearer than the first-place ballots suggest; I would be glad to hear whether the STEM question is a bar or only a refinement of the citation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for the prediction-then-experiment sequence and for the controllable correlated-electron platform it opened.
responses.response: The theory-experiment sequence is attractive, and I ranked it fourth. However, you, Lindroth and Mehlig all note that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that the experimental credit extends beyond the supplied names, including Cao as first author. That seems to me a maturity and attribution problem that circuit QED does not share, so I would wait on moire matter rather than treat it as ready now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges circuit QED sufficiently distinct from the 2025 macroscopic-tunnelling prize, or prefers to leave a longer interval.
Whether Girvin, Huang or the wider Yale team should alter the trio, which cannot be settled from the supplied credited names.
Whether the sharp rival, optical lattice clocks, would win if the redefinition of the second takes place before the decision.
How IceCube would fare if colleagues outside astroparticle physics were to examine the source-identification evidence, since only two members ranked it.
statement.conflict_note: My documented connections are to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur and to the KTH astroparticle group. I have no documented tie to circuit QED. IceCube (B040) is my own field of astroparticle physics and I have no documented collaboration with it, but that proximity should be borne in mind when weighing my earlier first-place ranking. No specific recusal conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
